claim: Base excision repair (BER) functions in the maintenance of genomic integrity.
source: Base excision repair (BER) functions not only in the maintenance of genomic integrity but also in active DNA demethylation and epigenetic gene regulation.
evidence: This is a well-established scientific fact about BER function, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Base excision repair (BER) functions in active DNA demethylation and epigenetic gene regulation.
source: Base excision repair (BER) functions not only in the maintenance of genomic integrity but also in active DNA demethylation and epigenetic gene regulation.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and cited literature in the field.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 act in repair of oxidative lesions.
source: Here we investigate the bifunctional DNA glycosylases/lyases NEIL1 and NEIL2, which act in repair of oxidative lesions and in epigenetic demethylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Bandaru et al., 2002; Hazra et al., 2002a; Hazra et al., 2002b; Takao et al., 2002) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 act in epigenetic demethylation.
source: Here we investigate the bifunctional DNA glycosylases/lyases NEIL1 and NEIL2, which act in repair of oxidative lesions and in epigenetic demethylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research (Müller et al., 2014; Schomacher et al., 2016; Slyvka et al., 2017; Spruijt et al., 2013) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: Neil-deficiency in Xenopus embryos leads to a defect in cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) development.
source: Neil-deficiency in Xenopus embryos and differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) leads to a surprisingly restricted defect in cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neil-deficiency in differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) leads to a defect in cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) development.
source: Neil-deficiency in Xenopus embryos and differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) leads to a surprisingly restricted defect in cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neil-deficiency elicits an oxidative stress-induced TP53-dependent DNA damage response.
source: Neil-deficiency elicits an oxidative stress-induced TP53-dependent DNA damage response, which impairs early cNCC specification.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including Western blots, qPCR, and RNA-seq analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: The TP53-dependent DNA damage response impairs early cNCC specification.
source: Neil-deficiency elicits an oxidative stress-induced TP53-dependent DNA damage response, which impairs early cNCC specification.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including rescue experiments with tp53 MO shown in Figure 4.

claim: Epistasis experiments with Tdg-deficient mESCs show no involvement of epigenetic DNA demethylation in Neil-deficiency phenotypes.
source: Epistasis experiments with Tdg-deficient mESCs show no involvement of epigenetic DNA demethylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Tdg-deficiency does not affect cNCC differentiation and does not rescue Neil1-deficiency phenotypes (Figure 9).

claim: Neil-deficiency results in oxidative damage specific to mitochondrial DNA.
source: Instead, Neil-deficiency results in oxidative damage specific to mitochondrial DNA, which triggers a TP53-mediated intrinsic apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS quantification of DNA damage and long-range PCR data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA triggers a TP53-mediated intrinsic apoptosis.
source: Instead, Neil-deficiency results in oxidative damage specific to mitochondrial DNA, which triggers a TP53-mediated intrinsic apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing changes in Bcl2 and Bak1 expression, and rescue experiments with Pifithrin-α (Figures 2, 12).

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 DNA glycosylases protect mitochondrial DNA against oxidative damage during neural crest differentiation.
source: Thus, NEIL1 and NEIL2 DNA glycosylases protect mitochondrial DNA against oxidative damage during neural crest differentiation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including DNA damage quantification and rescue experiments.

claim: TET dioxygenases iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).
source: The best understood active demethylation mechanism involves TET dioxygenases, which iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TET dioxygenases iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-formylcytosine (5fC).
source: The best understood active demethylation mechanism involves TET dioxygenases, which iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009), 5-formylcytosine (5fC) (Ito et al., 2011; Pfaffeneder et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TET dioxygenases iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC).
source: The best understood active demethylation mechanism involves TET dioxygenases, which iteratively oxidize the methyl group at C5 to yield 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009), 5-formylcytosine (5fC) (Ito et al., 2011; Pfaffeneder et al., 2011), and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) (He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG) excises 5fC and 5caC.
source: Thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG) excises 5fC and 5caC and the ensuing abasic site intermediate is processed by BER to restore unmethylated C (Cortázar et al., 2011; Cortellino et al., 2011; He et al., 2011; Maiti and Drohat, 2011; Shen et al., 2013; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The abasic site intermediate produced by TDG is processed by BER to restore unmethylated C.
source: Thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG) excises 5fC and 5caC and the ensuing abasic site intermediate is processed by BER to restore unmethylated C (Cortázar et al., 2011; Cortellino et al., 2011; He et al., 2011; Maiti and Drohat, 2011; Shen et al., 2013; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Deficiency of BER enzymes (e.g. TDG, APEX1, POLB, LIG3, XRCC1) can lead to abnormalities or lethality during embryogenesis.
source: Deficiency of the BER enzymes (e.g. TDG, APEX1, POLB, LIG3, XRCC1) can lead to abnormalities or lethality during embryogenesis (Cortázar et al., 2011; Cortellino et al., 2011; Puebla-Osorio et al., 2006; Sugo et al., 2000; Tebbs et al., 1999; Xanthoudakis et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 process oxidative DNA base lesions.
source: These enzymes process oxidative DNA base lesions (Bandaru et al., 2002; Hazra et al., 2002a; Hazra et al., 2002b; Takao et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 have been implicated in the machinery that removes 5-methylcytosine (5mC) from DNA during epigenetic DNA demethylation.
source: but recently they have also been implicated in the machinery that removes 5-methylcytosine (5mC) from DNA during epigenetic DNA demethylation (Müller et al., 2014; Schomacher et al., 2016; Slyvka et al., 2017; Spruijt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 are bifunctional enzymes that excise damaged bases and introduce DNA single strand breaks via their AP lyase activity.
source: NEIL1 and NEIL2 are bifunctional enzymes, which not only excise the damaged base but introduce a DNA single strand break via their AP lyase activity (Hazra et al., 2002a; Hazra et al., 2002b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL3 is mainly a monofunctional DNA glycosylase.
source: while NEIL3 is mainly a monofunctional DNA glycosylase (Krokeide et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 is involved in prereplicative repair during S-phase.
source: NEIL1 is involved in prereplicative repair during S-phase (Hegde et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NEIL2 preferentially processes oxidized bases from transcribing genes via transcription-coupled BER.
source: and NEIL2 preferentially processes oxidized bases from transcribing genes via transcription-coupled BER (Banerjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: During epigenetic DNA demethylation NEIL1 and NEIL2 cooperate with TDG to excise oxidized 5mC intermediates generated by TET enzymes.
source: During epigenetic DNA demethylation NEIL1 and NEIL2 cooperate with TDG to excise oxidized 5mC intermediates generated by TET enzymes (Schomacher et al., 2016; Slyvka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mice deficient of NEIL1 are viable but display metabolic syndrome and brain dysfunction.
source: Mice deficient of NEIL1 are viable but display metabolic syndrome and brain dysfunction (Canugovi et al., 2012; Rolseth et al., 2017; Vartanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neil2 null mice are viable but are susceptible to inflammation.
source: Neil2 null mice are also viable but are susceptible to inflammation (Chakraborty et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neil2-deficient frog embryos display neural crest defects.
source: while Neil2-deficient frog embryos display neural crest defects (Schomacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Knockdown of Neil2 with an antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (neil2 MO) induces head and tail abnormalities at tailbud stage in Xenopus embryos.
source: We showed previously that in Xenopus embryos knockdown of Neil2 with an antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (neil2 MO) induces head and tail abnormalities at tailbud stage, which are caused by impaired cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) specification at neurula stage (Schomacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Head and tail abnormalities in neil2 MO-injected Xenopus embryos are caused by impaired cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) specification at neurula stage.
source: We showed previously that in Xenopus embryos knockdown of Neil2 with an antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (neil2 MO) induces head and tail abnormalities at tailbud stage, which are caused by impaired cranial neural crest cell (cNCC) specification at neurula stage (Schomacher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The specificity of the neil2 MO was documented by phenocopy with a second non-overlapping morpholino.
source: The specificity of the neil2 MO had been documented (Schomacher et al., 2016) i) by phenocopy with a second non-overlapping morpholino
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The specificity of the neil2 MO was documented by rescue of the head and tail abnormalities with orthologous human NEIL2 mRNA.
source: The specificity of the neil2 MO had been documented (Schomacher et al., 2016) i) by phenocopy with a second non-overlapping morpholino, and ii) by rescue of the head and tail abnormalities with orthologous human NEIL2 mRNA, which was not targeted by neil2 MO (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Human NEIL2 mRNA was not targeted by neil2 MO.
source: by rescue of the head and tail abnormalities with orthologous human NEIL2 mRNA, which was not targeted by neil2 MO (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Proper differentiation of cNCCs is crucial for the development of craniofacial cartilage and bone structures.
source: Proper differentiation of cNCCs is crucial for the development of craniofacial cartilage and bone structures (Sakai and Trainor, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neil2 MO-injected embryos revealed head cartilage defects at tadpole stage.
source: Indeed, Alcian blue staining of head cartilage in neil2 MO-injected embryos (single blastomere injection at 2-cell stage) revealed head cartilage, notably branchial cartilage defects at tadpole stage (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Head cartilage defects in neil2 MO-injected embryos were rescued by simultaneous injection of human NEIL2 mRNA.
source: which were rescued by simultaneous injection of human NEIL2 mRNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Differential expression analysis of neil2 MO-injected embryos yielded a similar number of a few hundred up- and downregulated genes.
source: Differential expression analysis yielded a similar number of a few hundred up- and downregulated genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of upregulated genes in neil2 MO-injected embryos revealed 'Tp53 pathway' and 'Tp53 pathway feedback loops' as top hits.
source: Interestingly, pathway enrichment analysis revealed significant results only for the upregulated genes with the top hits 'Tp53 pathway' and 'Tp53 pathway feedback loops' suggestive of a DNA damage response (DDR) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Protein levels of both Tp53 and its upstream regulator phospho-Chk1 (pChk1) were induced in neural plates of Neil2 morphants.
source: Indeed, protein levels of both Tp53 and its upstream regulator phospho-Chk1 (pChk1) were induced in neural plates of Neil2 morphants, indicative for a DDR (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed upregulation of tp53 and its target genes, including ccng1, eda2r, aen, and riok3 in Neil2 morphants.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed upregulation of tp53 and its target genes, including ccng1, eda2r, aen, and riok3 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Co-injection of human NEIL2 mRNA rescued induced pChk1 in Neil2 morphants.
source: Furthermore, co-injection of human NEIL2 mRNA rescued induced pChk1 in Neil2 morphants, ruling out an unspecific Tp53-response to MO injection (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Human NEIL2 mRNA reduced basal pChk1 levels.
source: Notably, human NEIL2 mRNA also reduced basal pChk1 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The DDR in Neil2 morphants induced direct Tp53 targets characteristic for apoptosis (e.g. eda2r, aen).
source: The DDR in Neil2 morphants induced direct Tp53 targets characteristic for apoptosis (e.g. eda2r, aen).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figures 1D and 1F.

claim: Ablation of Tp53 and concomitant block of apoptosis suppress cranial facial abnormalities in Tcof1 mouse mutants.
source: Apoptosis is linked to cNCC developmental defects since ablation of Tp53 and concomitant block of apoptosis suppress cranial facial abnormalities in Tcof1 mouse mutants (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cell proliferation seemed unaffected in neil2 MO-injected embryos as judged by phospho-histone H3 levels.
source: Indeed, while cell proliferation seemed unaffected in neil2 MO-injected embryos as judged by phospho-histone H3 levels (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Elevated Caspase-3 cleavage was observed in dissected neural plates but less in non-neural tissue of neil2 MO-injected embryos.
source: we observed elevated Caspase-3 cleavage in dissected neural plates but less in non-neural tissue (Figure 1I), indicative of cNCC-specific apoptosis in Neil2 morphants.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Human NEIL2 mRNA injection in Neil2 morphants rescued elevated Caspase-3 cleavage to endogenous levels.
source: Consistently, human NEIL2 mRNA injection in Neil2 morphants rescued elevated Caspase-3 cleavage to endogenous levels, corroborating the specificity of the neil2 MO-induced apoptosis in neural plates.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Human NEIL2 mRNA injection decreased basal levels of cleaved Caspase-3, both in neural plates and non-neural tissue.
source: Human NEIL2 mRNA injection also decreased basal levels of cleaved Caspase-3, both in neural plates and non-neural tissue (Figure 1I), suggesting that elevated Neil2 expression protects against apoptosis in whole embryos.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Whole mount TUNEL assay of unilaterally neil2 MO-injected embryos confirmed elevated apoptosis by Neil2-deficiency in stage 16 embryos.
source: Whole mount TUNEL assay of unilaterally neil2 MO-injected embryos confirmed elevated apoptosis by Neil2-deficiency in stage 16 embryos (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Neil2 protects against Tp53-mediated cell apoptosis in Xenopus embryos, notably in neural plate tissue.
source: We conclude that Neil2 protects against Tp53-mediated cell apoptosis in Xenopus embryos, notably in neural plate tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including Western blots, TUNEL assays, and rescue experiments.

claim: Bcl2l1 is a Xenopus homologue of mammalian BCL2, an anti-apoptotic factor acting downstream of TP53.
source: Bcl2l1 is a Xenopus homologue of mammalian BCL2, an anti-apoptotic factor acting downstream of TP53 (Hemann and Lowe, 2006; Tsujimoto, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bcl2l1 overexpression substantially reduced phenotypic abnormalities of Neil2 morphants.
source: Importantly, bcl2l1 overexpression substantially reduced phenotypic abnormalities of Neil2 morphants (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Bcl2l1 overexpression rescued elevated cleaved Caspase-3 levels in Neil2 morphants in a dose-dependent manner.
source: and rescued elevated cleaved Caspase-3 levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bcl2l1 expression had no effect on endogenous nor induced Tp53 protein levels.
source: As expected, bcl2l1 expression had no effect on endogenous nor induced Tp53 protein levels (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BCL2 regulates the intrinsic apoptosis pathway that is associated with mitochondria and results in mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: BCL2 regulates the intrinsic apoptosis pathway that is associated with mitochondria and results in mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCL2 function.

claim: Upregulation of mitochondrial (mt) gene expression is a characteristic response to mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Upregulation of mitochondrial (mt) gene expression is a characteristic response to mitochondrial dysfunction (Heddi et al., 1999; Reinecke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased expression of mt-Nd1,4 and 5 and mt-co3 was observed in Neil2-morphant whole embryos.
source: Indeed, we observed increased expression of mt-Nd1,4 and 5 (NADH dehydrogenase 1,4 and 5) and mt-co3 (cytochrome c oxidase III) in Neil2-morphant whole embryos, supporting ongoing intrinsic apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NEIL2 processes oxidative base lesions induced by reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as 8-oxoguanine (8oxoG), 5-hydroxyuracil (5hU), thymine glycol, and the formamidopyrimidines FapyG and FapyA.
source: NEIL2 processes oxidative base lesions induced by reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as 8-oxoguanine (8oxoG), 5-hydroxyuracil (5hU), thymine glycol, and the formamidopyrimidines FapyG and FapyA (Hailer et al., 2005; Jacobs and Schär, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Embryo treatment with the ROS producer pyocyanin upregulated Tp53 and pChk1 protein.
source: Embryo treatment with the ROS producer pyocyanin (Zhao et al., 2014) upregulated Tp53 and pChk1 protein (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pyocyanin treatment induced expression of tp53 and its target genes.
source: induced expression of tp53 and its target genes (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pyocyanin treatment elevated Caspase-3 cleavage.
source: and elevated Caspase-3 cleavage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pyocyanin-treated embryos phenocopied Neil2 morphants, displaying similar head and tail abnormalities.
source: Moreover, pyocyanin-treated embryos phenocopied Neil2 morphants, displaying similar head and tail abnormalities (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Pyocyanin-treated neurula stage embryos showed cNCC specification defects, where the cNCC markers sox10, twist, and snail2 were downregulated.
source: Neurula stage embryos showed cNCC specification defects, where the cNCC markers sox10, twist, and snail2 were downregulated, while the markers sox3 (pan-neural), en2 (midbrain), and rx1 (eye) were unaffected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The markers sox3 (pan-neural), en2 (midbrain), and rx1 (eye) were unaffected by pyocyanin treatment.
source: Neurula stage embryos showed cNCC specification defects, where the cNCC markers sox10, twist, and snail2 were downregulated, while the markers sox3 (pan-neural), en2 (midbrain), and rx1 (eye) were unaffected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Elevated ROS levels sensitized Neil2 morphants.
source: Elevated ROS levels sensitized Neil2 morphants since pyocyanin treatment of embryos injected with a sub-critical dose of neil2 MO, which alone did not yield abnormalities, elicited exacerbated abnormalities (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Neil2-deficiency and ROS damage induce a Tp53 DDR in Xenopus embryos, leading to cNCC defects.
source: We conclude that Neil2-deficiency and ROS damage induce a Tp53 DDR in Xenopus embryos, leading to cNCC defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including pyocyanin treatment experiments.

claim: Treatment of embryos with Vitamin C attenuated the severe malformations of Neil2 morphants.
source: Importantly, treatment of embryos with Vitamin C, a prominent antioxidant (Arrigoni and De Tullio, 2002), attenuated the severe malformations of Neil2 morphants (Figure 3G), supporting ROS as the basis of cNCC defects in the absence of Neil2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Among the most upregulated genes in Neil2 morphants was the direct Tp53 target gene cyclin-G1 (ccng1).
source: Among the most upregulated genes in Neil2 morphants was the direct Tp53 target gene cyclin-G1 (ccng1) (Supplementary file 1) (Okamoto and Beach, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citation to previous research.

claim: Ccng1 interacts with Mdm2 and is involved in a negative feedback loop regulating Tp53 protein levels induced by DNA damage.
source: Ccng1 interacts with Mdm2, another Tp53 target gene, and is involved in a negative feedback loop regulating Tp53 protein levels induced by DNA damage (Kimura and Nojima, 2002; Okamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Unilateral injection of neil2 MO in Xenopus embryos confirmed upregulation of ccng1 on the injected side.
source: Unilateral injection of neil2 MO in Xenopus embryos with the lineage tracer β-galactosidase confirmed upregulation of ccng1 on the injected side (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ccng1 induction was restricted to the neural plate even in embryos where the lineage tracer extended to mesoderm and endoderm.
source: Ccng1 induction was restricted to the neural plate even in embryos where the lineage tracer extended to mesoderm and endoderm (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pyocyanin induced strong ccng1 expression restricted to the neural plate.
source: To test if the spatial restriction of ccng1 expression reflects tissue-specificity of the DDR, we provoked a systemic DDR using pyocyanin, which induced strong ccng1 expression (Figure 4B). As observed in Neil2 morphants, ccng1 expression was spatially restricted to the neural plate.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tp53 is preferentially expressed in the neural plate, notably in the anterior wherefrom cNCCs arise.
source: Spatial restriction of the DDR may be related to patterned expression of tp53 itself, as in situ hybridization showed preferential tp53 expression in the neural plate, notably in the anterior wherefrom cNCCs arise (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High-level expression of tp53 in the embryonic CNS is observed in diverse vertebrates, including zebrafish, Xenopus, chick, and mouse.
source: High-level expression of tp53 in the embryonic CNS is observed in diverse vertebrates, including zebrafish, Xenopus, chick, and mouse (Hoever et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2008; Rinon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tp53 mRNA injection downregulated the cNCC marker snail2 at mid neurula stage.
source: Consistently, tp53 mRNA injection downregulated the cNCC marker snail2 at mid neurula stage (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tp53 mRNA injection induced head and tail abnormalities.
source: and induced head and tail abnormalities (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Injection of a tp53 antisense MO blocked induction of Tp53 target genes in Neil2 morphants.
source: Importantly, injection of a tp53 antisense MO (Takebayashi-Suzuki, 2003) not only blocked induction of Tp53 target genes in Neil2 morphants but also rescued phenotypic abnormalities substantially (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and phenotypic data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Injection of a tp53 antisense MO rescued phenotypic abnormalities in Neil2 morphants substantially.
source: Importantly, injection of a tp53 antisense MO (Takebayashi-Suzuki, 2003) not only blocked induction of Tp53 target genes in Neil2 morphants but also rescued phenotypic abnormalities substantially (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Neil2 protects against an oxidative DNA damage-induced Tp53 response and intrinsic apoptosis in the neural plate, thereby safeguarding cNCC development.
source: In sum, we propose that Neil2 protects against an oxidative DNA damage-induced Tp53 response and intrinsic apoptosis in the neural plate, thereby safeguarding cNCC development (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on multiple experimental results.

claim: APEX1 functions downstream of DNA glycosylases, processing the abasic (apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP)) sites produced during BER.
source: APEX1 (Apurinic/Apyrimidinic Endodeoxyribonuclease 1) functions downstream of DNA glycosylases, processing the abasic (apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP)) sites produced during BER (Abbotts and Madhusudan, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Apex1-deficiency in mice leads to early embryonic lethality.
source: and Apex1-deficiency in mice leads to early embryonic lethality (Xanthoudakis et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Injection of apex1 MO at similar dosage as neil2 MO induced severe abnormalities and early lethality.
source: Injection of apex1 MO at similar dosage as neil2 MO induced severe abnormalities and early lethality confirming essentiality of Apex1 also for Xenopus embryonic development (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Injection of reduced amounts of apex1 MO phenocopied Neil2 morphants, with embryos displaying microcephaly, and reduced or absent dorsal and tail fins.
source: Interestingly, injection of reduced amounts of apex1 MO phenocopied Neil2 morphants, with embryos displaying microcephaly, and reduced or absent dorsal and tail fins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human APEX1 mRNA partially rescued the apex1 MO phenotype.
source: Human APEX1 mRNA partially rescued the phenotype confirming specificity of the apex1 MO (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tp53 and phospho-Chk1 levels were unaltered in Apex1 morphants.
source: While Tp53 and phospho-Chk1 levels were unaltered (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tp53 target genes were induced in Apex1 morphants.
source: Tp53 target genes were induced in Apex1 morphants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Phospho-histone H3 levels were unchanged in Apex1 morphants.
source: As in Neil2 morphants, phospho-histone H3 levels were unchanged and Caspase-3 cleavage was induced (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Caspase-3 cleavage was induced in Apex1 morphants.
source: As in Neil2 morphants, phospho-histone H3 levels were unchanged and Caspase-3 cleavage was induced (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The BER enzymes Neil2 and Apex1 exhibit similar functions in Xenopus neural crest development.
source: Hence, the BER enzymes Neil2 and Apex1 exhibit similar functions in Xenopus neural crest development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similar phenotypes observed in Neil2 and Apex1 morphants.

claim: Neil1,2,3 triple-knockout (TKO) mESCs were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
source: We generated Neil1,2,3 triple-knockout (TKO) mESCs by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (Cong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the methods described and citation to the CRISPR/Cas9 technique.

claim: The biochemical and biological properties of NEIL3 are quite distinct from those of NEIL1 and NEIL2.
source: The biochemical and biological properties of NEIL3, however, are quite distinct from those of NEIL1 and NEIL2 (Krokeide et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Teratomas grew from all six mESC lines (control and Neil-TKO) when transplanted subcutaneously into immunodeficient mice.
source: When transplanted subcutaneously into immunodeficient mice, teratomas grew from all six mESC lines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Histological analysis of control and Neil-TKO teratomas revealed derivatives of ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm in all samples confirming pluripotency of Neil-deficient mESCs.
source: Histological analysis of control and Neil-TKO teratomas revealed derivatives of ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm in all samples confirming pluripotency of Neil-deficient mESCs (Figure 6A).

claim: Transcriptome analysis by RNA-seq uncovered thousands of genes differentially expressed between control and Neil-TKO teratomas.
source: However, transcriptome analysis by RNA-seq uncovered thousands of genes differentially expressed between control and Neil-TKO teratomas (Figure 6B).

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of >2 fold differentially expressed genes in Neil-TKO teratomas yielded 'PluriNetWork' as a significant hit for upregulated genes.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of >2 fold differentially expressed genes in Neil-TKO teratomas yielded 'neural crest differentiation' as a significant hit for downregulated genes.
source: Intriguingly, pathway enrichment analysis of >2 fold differentially expressed genes yielded one significant hit for the up- and downregulated genes each, 'PluriNetWork' and 'neural crest differentiation', respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Upregulation of pluripotency markers (Pou5f1, Nanog and Klf4) was confirmed in Neil-TKO teratomas.
source: We confirmed upregulation of pluripotency markers (Pou5f1, Nanog and Klf4), suggesting incomplete silencing of the pluripotent state in Neil-TKO teratomas (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Downregulated genes in Neil-TKO teratomas included neural crest effectors such as Pax3, Tfap2b, Phox2b, Dbh, Crabp1, Neurog1 and Wnt3a.
source: Downregulated genes included neural crest effectors such as Pax3 (LaBonne and Bronner-Fraser, 1998), Tfap2b, Phox2b, Dbh, Crabp1, Neurog1 and Wnt3a

claim: A suite of downregulated Hox genes (Hoxa2, Hoxa3, Hoxa4, Hoxa5, Hoxa9, Hoxb1, Hoxb2, Hoxb3, Hoxb4, Hoxb5, Hoxc4, Hoxc5, Hoxd3) were observed in Neil-TKO teratomas.
source: besides a suite of downregulated Hox genes (Hoxa2, Hoxa3, Hoxa4, Hoxa5, Hoxa9, Hoxb1, Hoxb2, Hoxb3, Hoxb4, Hoxb5, Hoxc4, Hoxc5, Hoxd3), which are prominently expressed during neural crest/pharyngeal arch patterning, where they control head skeletal development (Trainor and Krumlauf, 2001) (Supplementary file 2).

claim: Hox genes are prominently expressed during neural crest/pharyngeal arch patterning, where they control head skeletal development.
source: besides a suite of downregulated Hox genes (Hoxa2, Hoxa3, Hoxa4, Hoxa5, Hoxa9, Hoxb1, Hoxb2, Hoxb3, Hoxb4, Hoxb5, Hoxc4, Hoxc5, Hoxd3), which are prominently expressed during neural crest/pharyngeal arch patterning, where they control head skeletal development (Trainor and Krumlauf, 2001) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Marker gene analysis indicated mild neural and severe neural crest differentiation defects in Neil-TKO teratomas.
source: In fact, marker gene analysis for endoderm (Gata6), mesoderm (Eomes), neuroectoderm (Pax6, Nestin, Sox1 and Pax2), and neural crest (Pax3, Hoxa2, Tfap2b and Neurog1) indicated mild neural and severe neural crest differentiation defects (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: The TP53 target genes Ccng1, Mdm2, Sesn2 and Eda2r were significantly upregulated in Neil TKO teratomas.
source: Moreover, the TP53 target genes Ccng1, Mdm2, Sesn2 and Eda2r were significantly upregulated in Neil TKO teratomas (Figure 6F) indicative of a TP53 DDR.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The requirement for NEIL function in cNCC development is evolutionarily conserved between amphibians and mammals.
source: These results indicate that the requirement for NEIL function in cNCC development is evolutionarily conserved between amphibians and mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similar phenotypes observed in Xenopus and mouse models.

claim: Neil3 mutants were largely unaffected for all markers tested during in vitro differentiation.
source: Neil3 mutants were largely unaffected for all markers tested (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants showed significant reduction in neural crest marker expression.
source: In contrast, single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants showed significant reduction in neural crest marker (Pax3, Hoxa2, Tfapb2, Neurog1) and also pan-neuroectodermal marker (Pax6, Nestin, Sox1, Pax2) expression, while endoderm- and mesoderm markers were unaffected (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants showed significant reduction in pan-neuroectodermal marker expression.
source: In contrast, single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants showed significant reduction in neural crest marker (Pax3, Hoxa2, Tfapb2, Neurog1) and also pan-neuroectodermal marker (Pax6, Nestin, Sox1, Pax2) expression, while endoderm- and mesoderm markers were unaffected (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Endoderm- and mesoderm markers were unaffected in single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants.
source: In contrast, single Neil1 and Neil2 mutants showed significant reduction in neural crest marker (Pax3, Hoxa2, Tfapb2, Neurog1) and also pan-neuroectodermal marker (Pax6, Nestin, Sox1, Pax2) expression, while endoderm- and mesoderm markers were unaffected (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pax3 and Pax6 induction during differentiation was partially restored in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells by stable transfection with catalytically active human NEIL1 and NEIL2.
source: Importantly, Pax3 and Pax6 induction during differentiation was partially restored in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells by stable transfection with catalytically active- but not inactive human NEIL1- and NEIL2-encoding constructs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Pax3 and Pax6 induction during differentiation was not restored in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells by stable transfection with catalytically inactive human NEIL1 and NEIL2.
source: Importantly, Pax3 and Pax6 induction during differentiation was partially restored in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells by stable transfection with catalytically active- but not inactive human NEIL1- and NEIL2-encoding constructs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The rescue confirms specificity of the Neil knockout approach.
source: This rescue not only confirms specificity of the Neil knockout approach but also demonstrates that the neural and cNCC differentiation defects are not due to mutant mESCs having undergone irreversible changes/DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The neural and cNCC differentiation defects are not due to mutant mESCs having undergone irreversible changes/DNA damage.
source: This rescue not only confirms specificity of the Neil knockout approach but also demonstrates that the neural and cNCC differentiation defects are not due to mutant mESCs having undergone irreversible changes/DNA damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The rescue indicates an acute requirement for NEIL1 and NEIL2 during cNCC differentiation.
source: Instead, the rescue indicates an acute requirement for NEIL1 and NEIL2 during cNCC differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The number of differentially expressed genes increased in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells substantially upon differentiation to several thousand, notably in EBs treated with RA.
source: Upon differentiation, the number of DE genes increased in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient cells substantially to several thousand, notably in EBs treated with RA, with up- and downregulated genes equally distributed (Figure 7B and Supplementary file 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The majority of differentially expressed genes overlapped between Neil1 and −2 mutant EBs and EBs + RA.
source: The majority of DE genes overlapped between Neil1 and −2 mutant EBs and EBs + RA (Figure 7C), supporting functional commonality between NEIL1 and NEIL2.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated genes in Neil1 and Neil2 mutants revealed 'neural crest differentiation' as the top hit in both genotypes and in both differentiation regimes.
source: Importantly, pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated genes revealed 'neural crest differentiation' as the top hit in both genotypes and in both differentiation regimes (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In vitro differentiation of Neil1- and Neil2 single-mutant mESCs recapitulates neural and cNCC differentiation defects observed in Neil-TKO teratomas.
source: We conclude that in vitro differentiation of Neil1- and Neil2 single-mutant mESCs recapitulates neural and cNCC differentiation defects observed in Neil-TKO teratomas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overlap of downregulated genes and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The upregulated genes of both Neil1- and Neil2-deficient EBs + RA were significantly enriched for the pathway term 'TYROBP causal network'.
source: Besides, the upregulated genes of both Neil1- and Neil2-deficient EBs + RA were significantly enriched for the pathway term 'TYROBP causal network' (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C), associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C and citation to previous research.

claim: Expression of germ layer marker genes was reduced for all tested tissues in the Apex1-mutant line.
source: Expression of germ layer marker genes was reduced for all tested tissues in the Apex1-mutant line (Figure 8A), indicating a more severe differentiation defect than in Neil1 and Neil2 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed a substantial overlap of commonly deregulated genes between Neil1-, Neil2- and Apex1-deficient EBs treated with RA.
source: Yet, RNA-seq analysis revealed a substantial overlap of commonly deregulated genes between Neil1-, Neil2- and Apex1-deficient EBs treated with RA (Figure 8B–C and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 8B–C.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated genes in Apex1 EBs + RA resulted in 'neural crest development' as the top hit.
source: Moreover, pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated genes in Apex1 EBs + RA once again resulted in 'neural crest development' as the top hit (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Apex1-deficient mESCs substantially phenocopy cNCC differentiation defects of Neil mutants similar to Xenopus embryos.
source: Thus, Apex1-deficient mESCs substantially phenocopy cNCC differentiation defects of Neil mutants similar to Xenopus embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similar phenotypes and pathway enrichment results.

claim: Tdg-deficient mESCs had 3–4-fold increased genomic 5fC and 5caC levels.
source: As expected, Tdg-deficient mESCs had 3–4-fold increased genomic 5fC and 5caC levels (Shen et al., 2013; Steinacher et al., 2019), but they showed no change in pluripotency marker expression (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1E and citations to previous research.

claim: Tdg-deficient mESCs showed no change in pluripotency marker expression.
source: As expected, Tdg-deficient mESCs had 3–4-fold increased genomic 5fC and 5caC levels (Shen et al., 2013; Steinacher et al., 2019), but they showed no change in pluripotency marker expression (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tdg-deficient cells subjected to EB differentiation induced marker gene expression of all germ layers with no significant difference from control cells.
source: Moreover, Tdg-deficient cells subjected to EB differentiation induced marker gene expression of all germ layers with no significant difference from control cells (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Oxidative Tdg-dependent DNA demethylation is not required for early cNCC differentiation in embryoid bodies.
source: We conclude that oxidative Tdg-dependent DNA demethylation is not required for early cNCC differentiation in embryoid bodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Tdg-deficiency experiments.

claim: In the Neil1/Tdg double-knockout line there was no rescue of cNCC differentiation.
source: However, in the Neil1/Tdg double-knockout line there was no rescue of cNCC differentiation, while the Tdg-single mutant line expectedly showed normal neural and cNCC marker gene expression (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The differentiation defects induced by deficiency of Neils are independent of a role in oxidative DNA demethylation.
source: We conclude that the differentiation defects induced by deficiency of Neils are independent of a role in oxidative DNA demethylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Neil1/Tdg double-knockout experiments.

claim: Pyocyanin inhibited neural and cNCC gene expression upon RA-induced EB differentiation, without affecting endoderm or mesoderm differentiation.
source: Consistently, pyocyanin inhibited neural and cNCC gene expression upon RA-induced EB differentiation, without affecting endoderm or mesoderm differentiation (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Upon differentiation, TP53 target gene expression significantly increased in presence of pyocyanin compared to mock treatment.
source: In addition, upon differentiation, TP53 target gene expression significantly increased in presence of pyocyanin compared to mock treatment (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Oxidative stress impairs cNCC differentiation.
source: The results align with the observation that oxidative stress impairs cNCC differentiation (Chen and Sulik, 1996; Sakai and Trainor, 2016; Yan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 localize to- and maintain genomic stability in the nucleus as well as in mitochondria.
source: Since NEIL1 and NEIL2 localize to- and maintain genomic stability in the nucleus as well as in mitochondria (Hu et al., 2005; Mandal et al., 2012; Prakash and Doublié, 2015; Vartanian et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Steady state levels of endogenous abasic sites in DNA are more abundant than oxidative base damages.
source: Since steady state levels of endogenous abasic sites in DNA are more abundant than oxidative base damages (Swenberg et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: APEX1-treatment reduced endogenous abasic sites by two-fold in purified gDNA from mESCs.
source: APEX1-treatment of purified gDNA from mESCs reduced endogenous abasic sites by two-fold, from ~229.000 sites per genome to ~120.000 sites per genome.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Subsequent EndoIII incubation led to a statistically significant increase of ~29.000 abasic sites per genome.
source: Subsequent EndoIII incubation led to a statistically significant increase of ~29.000 abasic sites per genome (Figure 11—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Steady state levels of EndoIII-reactive DNA damage sites were ~8 fold lower than the level of abasic sites.
source: Thus, steady state levels of EndoIII-reactive DNA damage sites were ~8 fold lower than the level of abasic sites, in agreement with previous reports (Swenberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data and citation to previous research.

claim: Levels of endogenous abasic sites (without APEX1/EndoIII treatment) were unaffected by Neil1- and Neil2-deficiency in gDNA and mtDNA, regardless of whether mESCs were differentiated or not.
source: Levels of endogenous abasic sites (without APEX1/EndoIII treatment) were unaffected by Neil1- and Neil2-deficiency in gDNA and mtDNA, regardless of whether mESCs were differentiated or not (Figure 11—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was no significant increase in EndoIII-processed sites in gDNA from Neil1- and Neil2-knockout cells.
source: Likewise, there was no significant increase in EndoIII-processed sites in gDNA from Neil1- and Neil2-knockout cells (Figure 11B, top).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: In mtDNA from Neil1- and Neil2-deficient mESCs, EndoIII-created abasic sites were elevated only upon neural differentiation (EB + RA), but not in EBs or undifferentiated mESCs.
source: In contrast, in mtDNA from Neil1- and Neil2-deficient mESCs, EndoIII-created abasic sites were elevated only upon neural differentiation (EB + RA), but not in EBs or undifferentiated mESCs (Figure 11B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Long-range PCR revealed increased mtDNA damage in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient EBs treated with RA, and to lesser extend in EBs without RA.
source: Comparing Neil-deficient to control cells, this approach revealed increased mtDNA damage in EBs treated with RA, and to lesser extend in EBs without RA (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is supported by long-range PCR data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Significant upregulation of mitochondrial and nuclear genes encoding components of oxidative phosphorylation was detected in Neil1- and Neil2-knockout cells, specifically under EB + RA treatment.
source: Moreover, as in Xenopus embryos we detected significant upregulation of mitochondrial and nuclear genes encoding components of oxidative phosphorylation as sign of mitochondrial dysfunction in Neil1- and Neil2-knockout cells, specifically under EB + RA treatment (Figure 11D) (Babenko et al., 2018; Heddi et al., 1999; Reinecke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 11D and citations to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 are specifically required for processing of oxidative lesions occurring in mitochondrial DNA during neural differentiation.
source: Together, the results suggest that NEIL1 and NEIL2 are specifically required for processing of oxidative lesions occurring in mitochondrial DNA during neural differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mtDNA damage quantification and gene expression data.

claim: There was a ~ 40% overlap between the 116 top TP53 target genes and the upregulated genes in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant EBs + RA.
source: Indeed, we found a ~ 40% overlap between the 116 top TP53 target genes (Fischer, 2017) and the upregulated genes in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant EBs + RA (Figure 12A)
evidence: This is supported by gene overlap analysis shown in Figure 12A and citation to previous research.

claim: There was no significant overlap between the 116 top TP53 target genes and upregulated genes in Neil1- and Neil2-deficient EBs and mESCs.
source: but no significant overlap with Neil1- and Neil2-deficient EBs and mESCs (Figure 12—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by gene overlap analysis shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Differentiation of control mESCs in presence of the TP53 stabilizer NSC 146109 resulted in specific neural and cNCC differentiation defects, thus mimicking Neil-deficiency.
source: Furthermore, differentiation of control mESCs in presence of the TP53 stabilizer NSC 146109 (Berkson et al., 2005) resulted in specific neural and cNCC differentiation defects, thus mimicking Neil-deficiency (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B and citation to previous research.

claim: Upon Pifithrin-α treatment the neuronal marker Pax6 and neural crest marker Pax3 in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant EBs + RA regained expression levels of control cells.
source: Strikingly, upon Pifithrin-α treatment the neuronal marker Pax6 and neural crest marker Pax3 in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant EBs + RA regained expression levels of control cells, while endoderm and mesoderm differentiation was marginally inhibited in all tested genotypes (Figure 12C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: In control EBs + RA Pifithrin-α treatment did not affect Pax6 and Pax3 expression.
source: In control EBs + RA Pifithrin-α treatment did not affect Pax6 and Pax3 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: An upregulated TP53 DDR impairs neural and cNCC differentiation in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant cells.
source: We conclude that an upregulated TP53 DDR impairs neural and cNCC differentiation in Neil1- and Neil2-mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Pifithrin-α rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of the anti-apoptotic factor Bcl2 was strongly downregulated in Neil-mutant EBs and EBs + RA.
source: Expression of the anti-apoptotic factor Bcl2 was strongly downregulated in Neil-mutant EBs and EBs + RA, while expression of Bak1, a pro-apoptotic factor of the Bcl2 family (Graupner et al., 2011; Tsujimoto, 1998), was significantly induced in Neil-deficient EBs + RA (Figure 12D), consistent with an intrinsic/mitochondrial TP53 response.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 12D.

claim: Expression of Bak1, a pro-apoptotic factor of the Bcl2 family, was significantly induced in Neil-deficient EBs + RA.
source: Expression of the anti-apoptotic factor Bcl2 was strongly downregulated in Neil-mutant EBs and EBs + RA, while expression of Bak1, a pro-apoptotic factor of the Bcl2 family (Graupner et al., 2011; Tsujimoto, 1998), was significantly induced in Neil-deficient EBs + RA (Figure 12D), consistent with an intrinsic/mitochondrial TP53 response.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 12D and citations to previous research.

claim: Pifithrin-α treatment reversed repression of Bcl2 and induction of Bak1 in Neil-deficient EBs + RA.
source: Pifithrin-α treatment reversed repression of Bcl2 and induction of Bak1 in Neil-deficient EBs + RA, confirming a TP53-dependent regulation of both genes (Figure 12—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The apoptosis effector CASPASE-3 is induced upon- and required for mESC neural differentiation.
source: The apoptosis effector CASPASE-3 is induced upon- and required for mESC neural differentiation (Fujita et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Levels of CASPASE-3 (cleaved and uncleaved) were systematically decreased in Neil-deficient EBs + RA.
source: Concordantly, levels of CASPASE-3 (cleaved and uncleaved) were systematically decreased in Neil-deficient EBs + RA (Figure 12—figure supplement 2A), thus different from Caspase-3-effected apoptosis in Xenopus (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Levels of CASPASE-7, the alternative effector caspase of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, were unchanged in Neil-deficient EBs + RA.
source: Levels of CASPASE-7, the alternative effector caspase of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway (Lakhani et al., 2006), were unchanged (Figure 12—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2B and citation to previous research.

claim: There were no significant differences in cell cycle profiles between the control and Neil1- or Neil2-deficient cells.
source: However, while cell cycle profiles of EBs and EBs + RA were clearly distinguishable from mESCs (more G1-phase and fewer S- and G2/M-phase cells upon mESC differentiation; White and Dalton, 2005), there were no significant differences in cell cycle profiles between the control and Neil1- or Neil2-deficient cells, arguing against a TP53-induced cell cycle arrest (Figure 12—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Cell cycle effects are absent after forced TP53 induction in neural crest cells in mice.
source: In line, cell cycle effects are also absent after forced TP53 induction in neural crest cells in mice (Bowen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 function as mitochondrial DNA repair glycosylases to counteract an increased oxidative stress during neurogenesis.
source: Collectively, the results support a model in which NEIL1 and NEIL2 function as mitochondrial DNA repair glycosylases to counteract an increased oxidative stress during neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on multiple experimental results.

claim: NEIL1 and NEIL2 protect against a mitochondrial-induced TP53-DDR and an intrinsic apoptosis pathway, and safeguard neural differentiation.
source: Thereby, NEIL1 and NEIL2 protect against a mitochondrial-induced TP53-DDR and an intrinsic apoptosis pathway, and safeguard neural differentiation (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on multiple experimental results.

claim: One-third of all congenital birth defects are craniofacial malformations that arise by perturbations in cNCC development.
source: One-third of all congenital birth defects are craniofacial malformations that arise by perturbations in cNCC development (Sakai and Trainor, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: cNCC defects caused by NEIL1- and NEIL2-deficiency are attributable primarily to their role in protecting against oxidative DNA lesions, in particular of the mitochondrial genome, rather than in promoting epigenetic DNA demethylation.
source: Our study indicates that cNCC defects caused by NEIL1- and NEIL2-deficiency are attributable primarily to their role in protecting against oxidative DNA lesions, in particular of the mitochondrial genome, rather than in promoting epigenetic DNA demethylation.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Neil1 mutants present metabolic syndrome and show impaired brain function and neuronal stress resistance in adults.
source: Neil1 mutants present metabolic syndrome and show impaired brain function and neuronal stress resistance in adults (Canugovi et al., 2012; Canugovi et al., 2015; Vartanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neil2-null mice are susceptible to innate inflammation.
source: Neil2-null mice are susceptible to innate inflammation (Chakraborty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neil1,2,3 triple-mutant mice were reported to be viable but negative for cancer predisposition.
source: Neil1,2,3 triple-mutant mice were recently reported to be viable, but mice were only analyzed- and reported negative for cancer predisposition (Rolseth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: cNCC development showed a surprisingly specific vulnerability towards NEIL-deficiency both in Xenopus embryos (Neil2) as well as in differentiating mESCs (NEIL1 and NEIL2).
source: In contrast, we found that cNCC development showed a surprisingly specific vulnerability towards NEIL-deficiency both in Xenopus embryos (Neil2) as well as in differentiating mESCs (NEIL1 and NEIL2).
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Deficiency of NEIL3 had no effect on neural and cNCC development.
source: Deficiency of NEIL3, which processes a different spectrum of lesions compared to NEIL1 and NEIL2 and is not found in mitochondria (Prakash and Doublié, 2015), had no effect on neural and cNCC development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citation to previous research.

claim: In Xenopus embryos and mESCs, the mechanism was elucidated as a TP53-mediated DNA damage response, which induced apoptosis in Xenopus (Caspase-3-dependent) and mouse EBs (downregulation of Bcl2 and induction of Bak1) without major effects on the cell cycle in both model systems.
source: In Xenopus embryos and mESCs, we elucidated the mechanism as a TP53-mediated DNA damage response, which induced apoptosis in Xenopus (Caspase-3-dependent) and mouse EBs (downregulation of Bcl2 and induction of Bak1) without major effects on the cell cycle in both model systems.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: In Xenopus and mESCs elevated ROS reduced cNCC specification.
source: Moreover, in Xenopus and mESCs we found that elevated ROS reduced cNCC specification, supporting a conserved mechanism whereby an oxidative DNA damage response impairs cNCC differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pyocyanin treatment experiments.

claim: Apex1 mutant mESCs and Apex1 Xenopus morphants displayed cNCC differentiation defects.
source: Similarly, Apex1 mutant mESCs and Apex1 Xenopus morphants displayed cNCC differentiation defects, although gene misregulation (mESCs) and malformations (Xenopus) were more severe than in Neil-mutant mESCs and Neil2 morphants, consistent with early embryonic lethality of Apex1 mutant mice (Ludwig et al., 1998; Xanthoudakis et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 8 and citations to previous research.

claim: Neither did Tdg-deficiency affect cNCC differentiation in mESCs, nor did combined Tdg/Neil1-deficiency rescue cNCC differentiation defects.
source: In contrast, neither did Tdg-deficiency affect cNCC differentiation in mESCs, nor did combined Tdg/Neil1-deficiency rescue cNCC differentiation defects, arguing against oxidative DNA demethylation as the primary cause of the differentiation defect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Neurogenesis is accompanied by a metabolic switch from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation and, hence, escalated oxidative stress.
source: Neurogenesis is accompanied by a metabolic switch from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation and, hence, escalated oxidative stress (Khacho and Slack, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: High intrinsic ROS levels may render neural crest cells particularly vulnerable to oxidative DNA damage and thus dependent on efficient damage repair.
source: High intrinsic ROS levels may render neural crest cells particularly vulnerable to oxidative DNA damage and thus dependent on efficient damage repair.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the metabolic characteristics of neurogenesis.

claim: Neuroectoderm expresses high levels of DNA repair factors.
source: Consistently, neuroectoderm expresses high levels of DNA repair factors (Albino et al., 2011) and of Tp53 itself (Cheng et al., 1997; Hoever et al., 1994; Rinon et al., 2011); this study)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and data from this study.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA was identified as the primary target for oxidative DNA damage in the absence of NEIL1 and NEIL2 and specifically upon mESC neural differentiation.
source: Intriguingly, we identified mitochondrial DNA as the primary target for oxidative DNA damage in the absence of NEIL1 and NEIL2 and specifically upon mESC neural differentiation.
